prompts.L1:

Children picking up our bones Will never know that these were once As quick as foxes on the hill; And that in autumn, when the grapes Made sharp air sharper by their smell These had a being, breathing frost; And least will guess that with our bones We left much more, left what still is The look of things, left what we felt At what we saw. The spring clouds blow Above the shuttered mansion-house, Beyond our gate and the windy sky Cries out a literate despair. We knew for long the mansion's look And what we said of it became A part of what it is ... Children, Still weaving budded aureoles, Will speak our speech and never know, Will say of the mansion that it seems As if he that lived there left behind A spirit storming in blank walls, A dirty house in a gutted world, A tatter of shadows peaked to white, Smeared with the gold of the opulent sun.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Children, Will, And

outputs.L1:
Children picking up our bones  
Will never know that these were once  
As quick as foxes on the hill;  
And that in autumn, when the grapes  
Made sharp air sharper with their scent,  
These had a being, breathing frost.  

And least of all will they guess that, with our bones,  
We left much more: left what still is—  
The look of things; left what we felt  
At what we saw. The spring clouds blow  
Above the shuttered mansion-house,  
Beyond our gate; and the windy sky  
Cries out a literate despair.  

We knew for long the mansion’s look,  
And what we said of it became  
A part of what it is. Children,  
Still weaving budded aureoles,  
Will speak our speech and never know;  
Will say of the mansion that it seems  
As if he who lived there left behind  
A spirit storming in blank walls,  
A dirty house in a gutted world,  
A tatter of shadows peaked to white,  
Smeared with the gold of the opulent sun.
outputs.L2:
Children who one day gather our bones  
will not realize they once belonged to bodies  
swift like foxes running over the hills.  
They will not know that in autumn,  
when the scent of grapes made the cold air keener,  
these bones were part of living beings  
that drew breath in the frost.  

Even less will they understand  
that when we left our bones behind,  
we also left something greater:  
the appearance of the world as we knew it,  
and the feelings stirred in us  
by everything we saw.  

Spring clouds drift  
over the closed-up mansion,  
past our gate, while the blustery sky  
seems to cry out with a knowing sadness.  
For a long time we understood  
the face of that mansion,  
and the things we said about it  
became part of its meaning.  

Children, still forming bright halos of new buds,  
will use our words without knowing their source.  
They will say the mansion looks  
as though the person who once lived there  
left a restless spirit raging inside bare walls:  
a filthy house in a ruined world,  
a ragged cluster of shadows bleached pale,  
streaked with the rich gold  
of the extravagant sun.
outputs.L3:
Future generations will one day discover the speakers’ bones, but they will not be able to understand the life those bodies once contained. The remains may show that the speakers existed, yet they cannot reveal the full vitality, sensations, and experiences that once animated them. Their physical traces will survive, but the warmth of their perceptions—the way they saw, felt, and responded to the world—will be much harder to recover.

The speakers believe, however, that they have left behind more than bones. They imagine that their impressions of the world, their emotions, and their language will continue to linger after them. Their relationship with their surroundings has been so intense and sustained that it seems to have become part of the place itself. In particular, the mansion-house is not merely a building but a space shaped by memory, habit, and description. Through long familiarity, the speakers have given meaning to its rooms, its atmosphere, and its decay. The words they used to describe it have helped form the way the mansion will be perceived in the future.

As time passes, future children will unknowingly inherit this legacy. They may repeat the speakers’ language and impressions without realizing where those ideas came from. Their understanding of the mansion will be influenced by the perceptions left behind by earlier generations. In this way, the speakers’ voices will persist indirectly, carried forward through inherited phrases, attitudes, and images.

The mansion itself is presented as a haunted and decaying place. It is marked by emptiness, ruin, and fading beauty, suggesting both physical decline and emotional loss. Its grandeur has diminished, and what remains is a ghostly atmosphere filled with traces of the past. The house becomes a symbol of memory’s persistence: even as bodies decay and buildings fall into ruin, impressions, words, and feelings continue to haunt the future.
outputs.L4:
The poem is a meditation on mortality, inheritance, and the strange persistence of human perception after death. It imagines a future moment when children may discover the bones of the speakers, perhaps without knowing who they were or what kind of lives they lived. The physical body, in this vision, does not endure as a living presence; it becomes an object, a remnant, something that later generations might stumble upon. Yet the poem suggests that death does not completely erase a person’s influence. Even when the dead are unnamed and unrecognized, something of their inner life continues to shape the world inherited by those who come after them.

This inheritance is not simply material. The children do not merely find bones or occupy the same physical landscape. They also inherit ways of seeing, feeling, naming, and interpreting that were formed by the dead before them. The poem imagines that the perceptions once held by the speakers—the meanings they attached to certain places, objects, and experiences—will somehow pass into the consciousness of future generations. The children may believe their responses are entirely their own, but the poem implies that their vision has been quietly influenced by those who lived before them.

A central example is the mansion. To the children, the mansion may appear meaningful, mysterious, beautiful, or haunted, but they may not understand why it feels that way. The poem suggests that the emotional and imaginative associations surrounding the place have been created by earlier lives. The dead once looked at the mansion, thought about it, gave it significance, and filled it with language and feeling. Later generations then encounter not a neutral building, but a place already shaped by inherited meanings.

The poem’s key insight is that human beings leave behind more than bodies or possessions. They leave behind interpretations of the world. Their feelings, words, memories, and symbolic associations can survive them, entering the minds of others in ways that are indirect and unacknowledged. In this sense, the dead continue to participate in the living world. Although their bodies decay, their way of understanding reality becomes part of the atmosphere that future people breathe.

Ultimately, the poem presents inheritance as both intimate and mysterious. The children may never know the speakers, and they may not recognize the source of the thoughts and feelings they have received. Nevertheless, they are shaped by those earlier lives. The poem therefore treats mortality not as absolute disappearance, but as transformation: the self vanishes physically, yet its perceptions and meanings endure within the consciousness of others. Human life continues through the ways it teaches later generations to see.
outputs.L5:
**Children, Will, and the Future**

Children are the hope of every generation. Their dreams, curiosity, and energy shape the world they will one day lead. With care, education, and support, children can grow into confident people who make thoughtful choices and contribute positively to society.

Every child has a will of their own. This will helps them learn, explore, and overcome challenges. When adults listen to children and guide them with patience, children develop confidence and responsibility. They learn that their voices matter and that their actions can make a difference.

Families, schools, and communities all play an important role in helping children grow. Love and discipline, freedom and guidance, kindness and understanding must work together. When children are encouraged to think, ask questions, and believe in themselves, they will build a brighter future for everyone.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a modernist poem in the style of Wallace Stevens about mortality, children finding bones, autumn grapes, and a deserted mansion.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Grapes at the Empty House**

I

The children found the bones beneath the yew,  
Not skulls, not names, but ivory weatherings—  
A hinge of bird, a little moon of fox,  
The grammar of a creature once compelled  
To leap, to hunger, and to vanish there.

They held them up. The afternoon grew large.  
It was the hour when autumn, purple-mouthed,  
Leans on the trellis and invents the grape  
As if sweetness were a form of thought,  
As if decay could wear a lucid skin.

II

Beyond the orchard stood the mansion, shut.  
Its windows kept the color of old rain.  
No footman of the wind unlatched the door;  
No portrait turned its face from being gone.  
The rooms within were full of absent chairs,

And dust, that philosophic residue,  
Lay on the stair as calmly as a law.  
The children entered only with their eyes,  
Believing every house without a voice  
Must be the palace of a sleeping king.

III

But there was no king, unless the dead are kings,  
Unless the fallen leaf, in falling, reigns.  
The bones were small. The grapes were round and dark.  
A wasp went in and out of sweetness there,  
A yellow doubt among the purple proofs.

What is it, then, to perish? Not to end,  
But to become the weather of another thing:  
The chalk in a child’s palm, the wine-dark bead  
That tightens on the vine, the vacant hall  
Where sunlight practices its silent scales.

IV

The children laughed and scattered down the path,  
Carrying death as lightly as a shell.  
Behind them, in the mansion’s mirrored gloom,  
The autumn gathered up its robes of gold  
And stepped, leaf after leaf, into the air.

The grapes remained, the bones, the house, the sky—  
Each one a thought the earth had almost said.  
And evening, with its blue extinguishing,  
Made of the world no lesson and no wound,  
Only a shape, superb because it fades.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a lyrical free-verse poem where future children encounter the remains of the dead and unknowingly inherit their language and perceptions of a shuttered house.
counterfactuals.output:
After the last roof sighs inward,  
after rain learns the stairwell  
and moss takes the names from the mailbox,  

children come.

They are born past the season of anyone’s remembering,  
their pockets full of seed husks and blue glass,  
their hair smelling of smoke from kinder fires.  
They find the house shuttered against a sun  
that no longer asks permission to enter.

At first they think it is a sleeping animal—  
black ribs, blind eyes,  
a mouth hinged with rust.  
They press their palms to the door  
and feel, beneath the grain,  
the cooled pulse of rooms.

Inside, the dead have become patient.

A hand in the wall,  
a jaw beneath the pantry boards,  
buttons like small moons in the ash.  
The children kneel, not afraid,  
and lift the bones as if lifting syllables  
from a page softened by weather.

They do not know these were once mothers  
who leaned at the window listening for rain,  
or fathers who carried winter in their coats,  
or lovers who spoke low in the dark  
so grief would not wake.

They do not know the skulls  
held whole orchards of seeing—  
the sour shine of apples,  
the dust turning gold in afternoon,  
the particular mercy of a lamp  
left burning in the hall.

But when the children open their mouths,  
old words fly out.

Threshold.  
Hearth.  
Beloved.  
Storm.

They say them wrongly at first,  
with the accents of creek water and crows,  
yet the house shivers  
as if recognized.

One child names the window longing  
and suddenly sees how the shutters  
were not just closed  
but bracing themselves  
against years of departure.

Another calls the cellar sorrow  
and knows, without knowing,  
the smell of potatoes, damp wool,  
secrets stored in jars.

A third whispers home  
over the scattered ribs,  
and the floorboards answer  
with the creak of someone turning  
in an upstairs bed.

All day they gather the dead  
into baskets of fern and nettle.  
All day the dead give back  
what they can no longer carry:

the habit of looking west at dusk,  
the fear of empty chairs,  
the way dust resembles memory  
when light enters sideways,  
the belief that every locked room  
is keeping a breath inside.

By evening the children speak  
in the grammar of hinges,  
in the tense of portraits,  
in the plural of footsteps fading.  
They see the house  
not as ruin,  
but as a sentence interrupted—  
its shutters dark commas,  
its chimney a throat  
that once released winter’s black hymn.

They sleep beneath the collapsed rafters.  
Around them, the dead lie quiet,  
relieved of their nouns.

And in their dreams  
the children walk from room to room,  
touching the walls with borrowed hands,  
calling each absence by its tender name,

until morning lifts the roofless house  
into the pale, unshuttered air,

and they wake seeing  
as the vanished saw:

that every dwelling is made  
of those who could not stay,  
and every child is fluent  
in a language  
they never chose  
but carry.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a bleak, imagistic poem about bones, memory, spring clouds, a windy sky, and an abandoned mansion-house, using elevated early-20th-century diction.
counterfactuals.output:
Upon the hill the mansion-house decays,  
Its blinded windows full of ashen light;  
About its doors the nettle’s spectral blaze  
Leans in the wind that labours into night.  

There, under floors where rain has made its bed,  
The bones keep counsel with a little dust;  
Pale, patient relics of the vanished dead,  
They whiten where the joists give up their trust.  

Memory, like a servant long dismissed,  
Returns and moves through corridors of air,  
Lifting the mouldering arras of the mist  
To find no face, no footstep waiting there.  

Above, the spring clouds wander, cold and vast,  
Young clouds, yet grey with some ancestral doom;  
They trail their luminous tatters from the past  
Across the windy sky’s unquiet room.  

O broken house, thy chimneys stand like bones;  
Thy garden, choked with rain, forgets the rose;  
Only the gale, among the loosened stones,  
Repeats what no surviving creature knows.  

And when the dusk descends with hollow breath,  
The clouds go by like thoughts no soul can save;  
Spring flowers shiver at the edge of death,  
And memory lies down beside the grave.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poem that sounds like a lost Wallace Stevens piece, with themes of death, perception, inherited speech, and a ruined opulent house in a changing world.
counterfactuals.output:
**The House of Ancestral Weather**

I

The chandeliers, being dead, continue light.  
Their crystal pears, unplucked from smoky boughs,  
Repeat the moon in morsels, as a tongue  
Repeats the syllables it cannot own.

Outside, the lindens practice their green decline.  
The road goes modernly past the broken gates.  
A motor coughs where once the phaeton  
Made summer ceremonial with dust.

Who lived here lived in mirrors and in nouns:  
Blue room, west stair, the porcelain vestibule,  
The aunt’s French clock, the colonel’s lacquered cane—  
A speech inherited like silver forks,

Too bright for hunger, yet arranged for use.

II

Death is the butler who has kept the keys.  
He knows the cellar where the vintages  
Have turned to vinegar and violet shade.  
He knows the nursery with its paper birds

Still flying east upon a peeling wall.  
He wears no livery now. His cuffs are ash.  
He does not answer when the bell-pull swings  
In the immense politeness of the wind.

We say the dead are gone, but saying so  
Is one more furniture they left behind.  
The sentence stands, a cabinet of dark,  
Full of their linen, lavender, and bones.

The mouth is not a maker but a room  
Through which old voices pass and are perceived.

III

Perception is a sovereign ruin here.  
The eye invents a feast from broken plates,  
A peacock from the mold upon the stair,  
A music from the rain’s repeated nail.

One sees, and seeing is the old estate  
Transformed by looking into what it lacks.  
The fountain’s dry, yet in its basin lies  
A sky sufficient for a drowning god.

The statues, cracked by winters of new laws,  
Lean out from laurel, blind with marble sleep.  
Their blankness has the splendor of a mask  
Removed from no one, kept for no return.

What is the world but what the mind must wear  
When all its wardrobes of resemblance fail?

IV

The heirs have sold the orchard to the town.  
A school will rise where apricots once burned.  
The greenhouse panes, like arguments, are smashed;  
The roses go democratic in weeds.

Children will shout where portraits kept their lips  
Compressed against the varnish of descent.  
They will not know the names, and in not knowing  
Will make a cleaner music of the air.

Yet some phrase, fallen from a governess,  
Some reprimand in lace, some biblical  
Blue thunder of a grandfather at dusk,  
Will cling to them like pollen from these rooms.

No speech is new. The newness is the sun  
Discovering an old word on the tongue.

V

At evening, when the house becomes its loss,  
The windows darken into inward seas.  
The west, that gaudy undertaker, draws  
Gold curtains over acres of decay.

A fox goes through the ballroom, red and real.  
His paws disturb the dust of minuets.  
He pauses where the dowager’s gilt chair  
Has shed its arms like a defeated throne.

There is no moral in his narrow face.  
There is the fact of fur, the living flame,  
The sumptuous hunger moving through a hall  
Once built to keep such hunger out of sight.

The world is changed. It always was. The change  
Is merely visible, and therefore true.

VI

O house of adjectives, collapsed in rain,  
O grammar of possession, dispossessed,  
Your cornices still flourish in the mind  
Like phrases too magnificent to mean.

We enter you by speaking. We depart  
By seeing that the spoken is a door.  
Beyond it, death stands plainly in the grass,  
Not as conclusion, but as cold exactness—

The final clarity that does not speak,  
The black perception without metaphor.  
And yet the swallows scribble in the dusk,  
As if the air required handwriting still.

The chandeliers, being dead, continue light.  
Not light itself, but memory of glass:  
A brilliance we inherit and mistake  
For dawn, until the dawn revises us.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a literary poem beginning with children picking up our bones and ending with an image of shadows smeared with the gold of the sun.
counterfactuals.output:
Children picking up our bones  
will think us light as reeds,  
will turn our ribs like harps  
and listen for the weather  
we kept hidden there.

They will not know our names,  
only the chalky alphabet  
of knuckle, tooth, and spine;  
how we loved in rooms of rain,  
how we broke bread, broke vows,  
broke open like fruit  
beneath the ordinary moon.

They will carry us in baskets  
past the nettles and the stones,  
past the house where silence  
learned to sleep in every chair,  
and one will lift a skull  
as if it were a lantern  
emptied of its flame.

O small inheritors,  
forgive the dust we made.  
We planted wars like orchards,  
we drank the rivers down,  
we taught the earth our hunger  
and called it by our names.

Still, there were mornings  
when the world was merciful—  
a kettle singing, linen breathing,  
your mother’s hand in mine  
before you had a mother,  
before the dark had gathered  
its black wool at the door.

Lay us beneath the grass.  
Let rain revise us.  
Let roots take up the last  
white grammar of our bodies  
and speak us into leaves.

Then run home through the fields,  
where evening lowers its bright veil,  
and all along the road  
the shadows are smeared with the gold of the sun.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
